newsitem.title: GERMANY: German govt rejects proposal to limit Iran ties.
newsitem.headline: German govt rejects proposal to limit Iran ties.

text.p: The ruling German coalition on Friday dismissed Iran's claim it exerts political influence over German courts, but stopped short of agreeing to opposition demands to curtail exports and diplomatic ties with Tehran.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right government said it could not accept the threats made against a German prosecutor who charged Iran's leaders with ordering the 1992 shootings of three Kurdish dissidents and their translator in Berlin.
In a resolution approved by parliament, the government rejected Tehran's charges that the so-called "Mykonos trial" in Berlin was an example of "political justice".
Speakers from all the major parties in parliament said the sabre-rattling by Iran, including death threats against the federal prosecutor, was unacceptable.

But the coalition blocked a resolution proposed by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens that would have urged the government to freeze arms exports to Iran and limit diplomatic ties to a minimum.
"Normal diplomatic relations are still needed, but the more extensive forms of cooperation can no longer be permitted," said SPD parliamentarian Christoph Zoepel.
The debate in Bonn came as a senior Iranian cleric in Tehran said Iranians would not tolerate German charges that Tehran leaders had ordered political killings.

"The (Iranian) people are ready to see themselves wounded and shot at but they are not ready to tolerate any insult to their sanctities," Ayatollah Ahmad Jannati said in a mass prayer sermon broadcast live on state-run Tehran radio.
"Well, you saw Salman Rushdie's fate after that insult and rudeness," Jannati said.

Rushdie, a British novelist, has lived in hiding since 1989 when Iran's late spiritual leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini ordered his killing for allegedly blaspheming Islam in his novel "The Satanic Verses".

"We shall strongly insist on our positions and values and will not surrender to any judge or court," Jannati, a senior cleric known for his fiery rhetoric, told worshippers gathered at Tehran University.

In Berlin, the Iranian charged with masterminding the 1992 assassination said there was no evidence that he planned the murder or was involved in it. He is on trial with four Lebanese for the restaurant shootings.

In a personal statement handed to the Berlin court hearing closing arguments of the three-year-long trial, Kazem Darabi said his lawyer would not make a closing statement because, Darabi said, he was innocent.
